pages.title: What Is Waste?
pages.content:
Every day, we use many different things. We eat food, drink from plastic or glass bottles, and buy items in paper boxes and plastic packaging. Then, we often throw away leftover food, empty bottles, and old boxes. We call this waste. It is anything that we do not want or need anymore.

Today, people around the world create a huge amount of waste. In 2023, people in cities created more than 2 billion tons of waste. By 2050, this number could reach nearly 4 billion tons. That is a big problem.

Most city waste is food. Paper, cardboard, and plastic come next. Plastic waste is growing very fast, and a lot of it ends up in rivers and seas.

However, waste is not just a problem. We can also see it as a useful resource. Many of the things we throw away are still good. So, we can collect and reuse them. Different types of waste need different ways of collecting and recycling.

pages.title: Paper, Wood and Glass
pages.content:
Paper is made from forest trees, so recycling it helps us save more trees. Because used paper needs to stay dry, we should put it in a separate recycling bin. At recycling centers, this old paper is turned into new paper and cardboard boxes.

Wood also comes from trees, and we use it to make furniture, boxes, and even houses. Recycling centers can turn old wood into new wooden boards. That way, we can reuse it instead of throwing it away.

Glass is made from sand and other natural materials. We collect used bottles and jars in special recycling bins. At the center, workers group the glass by color and melt it to make new ones. This helps us save natural materials and make less trash.

pages.title: Plastic
pages.content:
Plastic is everywhere. We find it in bags, bottles, toys, phones, and many other things. However, there are many different types of plastic, and we cannot recycle all of them in the same way.

So what happens to all this plastic waste? Let’s look at the numbers from 2019. Only 9 percent of it was recycled, and 19 percent was burned in special places. Half of it went under the ground into big trash areas. The other 22 percent stayed in open places or went into nature. A lot of it ended up in rivers and seas. That is why plastic waste is such a big problem today.

pages.title: Cartons and Metal
pages.content:
Juice and milk cartons are made of paper and plastic, and some also have a thin layer of metal inside. Because we use these cartons every day, we create a lot of trash. We need to put them in a separate bin. At special centers, workers separate the paper and plastic, and then use them to make new things.

We dig metal out of the earth. Drink cans, oil cans, and tomato paste cans are all metal trash. We collect metal in a separate bin, too. At recycling centers, workers melt the metal and use it to make new products.

Is recycling metal a good idea? Yes, it is! It takes much less energy than getting new metal from the earth.

pages.title: Cooking Oil and Food
pages.content:
We make cooking oil from plants like olives, sunflowers, and corn. After we fry food, this used oil becomes waste, too. Because it can make our water dirty, we need to collect it separately. Special centers turn it into a clean fuel for cars and trucks. This fuel is called biodiesel.

Food waste comes from fruit and vegetable pieces, old bread, and other leftover food. Farms also have plant waste, like wheat and barley straw.

Sadly, a lot of food never reaches our tables. About 13 percent of the world’s food is lost on the way from the farm to the shop. 17 percent more is wasted in homes, restaurants, and shops. In fact, most of this wasted food—61 percent—comes from our homes!

pages.title: Electronics and Batteries
pages.content:
We use many electronic devices at home, at school, and at work. Fridges, washing machines, computers, and mobile phones make our lives easier. When they are no longer useful, they become electronic waste. Electronic waste has dangerous materials inside, so we must put it in special bins. Workers take these old devices apart, and then they can use the metal, plastic, and other useful parts again.

Batteries store energy and give power to many things. When a battery is no longer useful, it becomes battery waste. Never throw batteries in the regular bin! They have dangerous chemicals inside that can get into the soil and water. We must put old batteries in special battery bins. Then, recycling centers take out useful metals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel.

Recycling saves many useful materials, but it also needs a lot of energy and hard work. So, recycling alone cannot solve the problem. We need a better idea. This idea is Zero Waste.

pages.title: What Is Zero Waste?
pages.content:
Does “Zero Waste” mean “no waste at all”? No, that is not possible. We all use things and produce waste every day.

Zero Waste is a way of living. It means using things carefully and creating less waste. We should try not to throw things away, use them again and again, and recycle. With Zero Waste, we should think about the full life of what we buy. This helps us see that old items can still be useful.

Why is this so important? Every year, people around the world create more than 2 billion tons of waste. A lot of this waste is still valuable, so when we throw it away, we lose useful materials. Waste also pollutes the air, water, and soil. This is dangerous for both our health and nature.

pages.title: The Circular Economy
pages.content:
Zero Waste helps us build a circular economy. To understand the circular economy, first we should look at the old system.

The old system is like a line. It has three steps: take, make, and throw away. First, we take materials from nature, then we use them to make things, and finally, we throw them away. This is called a linear economy.

A circular economy is different. It works like a circle. In nature, nothing is wasted, and everything is used again and again. A circular economy works in the same way.

We use things and materials for as long as possible. Then, old things are turned into new products. They go round and round in a circle, so they do not end up in waste areas.

The main goal is simple: the economy can grow, but nature does not have to pay the price.

pages.title: The Three Rs
pages.content:
Zero Waste has three main rules. We call them the three Rs.

Reduce: Use less. Buy only the things you really need.

Reuse and Repair: Use things again and again instead of throwing them away. Companies should make good, strong products that are easy to repair. When something breaks, fix it. Then, it lasts longer, and you save money, too.

Recycle and Upcycle: Recycling means making new materials from old ones. For example, old paper becomes new paper. This saves natural materials, and less waste goes to landfills. Upcycling means turning waste into something new and more useful.

The circular economy helps us in three ways. First, there is less waste and pollution. Second, we use natural materials more carefully. Third, the economy grows, and there are new jobs in recycling and repair.

pages.title: Waste and Our Climate
pages.content:
Waste and climate change are closely connected. When food and other natural waste go bad under a lot of trash in big waste areas, they form a gas called methane. Methane is a greenhouse gas, and greenhouse gases make the Earth warmer. Because of this, ice melts fast, and extreme weather becomes more common.

Today, greenhouse gas levels are more than twice as high as they were 50 years ago. Zero Waste can help with this, too. When there is less trash in waste areas, waste creates fewer of these dangerous gases.

Better waste management can cut these gases by 15 to 20 percent. We need to act fast because we face a big problem and a very unfair situation. Many poorer countries create very little of these gases, yet they often suffer the most from climate change. They face terrible natural disasters, and sea levels are rising there.

pages.title: What Can We Do?
pages.content:
The best waste is the waste we never create. So, we need to be careful with what we buy and use.

We can start by buying only the food we need. We can shop at local markets and in stores that do not use plastic packaging. We can also say “no” to things we use only once, like paper coffee cups, plastic water bottles, and plastic straws. Making better choices is easy—for example, we can bring our own cups and bottles.

Cities can help, too. They can set up free water stations where people can fill up their bottles. They can support second-hand shops for clothes, furniture, and electronics. They can also help people repair broken things. Some cities even have tool libraries where people can borrow tools instead of buying them.

Children and their families can learn about Zero Waste together. This is the best way to change our daily habits, and the best time to start is now!

Zero Waste is not a finish line where we arrive and stop. It is a way of thinking, and the journey never ends.

exercises.explanation: After must, use the base verb. The past of go is went. Use “than” to compare.

feedback.incorrect: Check the verb and the comparison.

exercises.title: Use: A New Context
exercises.instructions: Read about a school fair. Fill each gap from the word bank.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s words in a new text?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Our class made a Zero Waste fair. First, we [blank] old toys and books from our families. Then we [blank] them by size. Some toys were broken, so we [blank] them. Visitors could [blank] books and bring them back later.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s words in a new text.
feedback.incorrect: Read the words around each gap.

exercises.title: Use: Check a Short Text
exercises.instructions: A student wrote about waste at home. Find each mistake.
exercises.question: What should the student change?

errorItems.sentence: Never to throw old batteries in the trash.
We try not buy plastic bottles.
Old oil can makes water dirty.

exercises.explanation: Use the base verb after Never and can. Use “try not to + verb”.

feedback.correct: Correct. Never throw, try not to buy, can make.
feedback.incorrect: Check the verb after each word.

exercises.title: Use: My Zero Waste Week
exercises.instructions: Write four to five sentences about your Zero Waste week.
exercises.question: What will you do, and why?
exercises.explanation: Example: “This week, I will use less plastic. I will take my own bottle to school every day. I will repair my old jacket. I will put paper in the recycling bin. This is important because the best waste is the waste we never create.”

feedback.correct: Check: reduce, reuse or repair, and because.
